title: Racing Hearts
sub: Grades 5–8 · PE · Your pulse, your alarm and the rustling bushes
objective: Poster 1 says that when you reach into a box you can’t see into, *“your heart races before you even touch anything.”* Students will measure that for themselves: their own pulse at rest, after waiting on a closed box, after a running game built on the lab’s *Rustling Bushes*, and after a calm minute. Through the game they will feel the poster’s trade-off, that it is *“better to see 100 fake threats than miss one real predator,”* and count what each kind of mistake costs.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Your heart answers fear and exercise alike. Knowing how to read it, and how to settle it, is a skill for every game, test and stage.

items.text: find and count your own pulse, and record it at rest, after waiting, after exercise and after a calm minute
items.question: find and count your pulse, and record it?

items.text: explain why your brain would rather raise a fake alarm than miss a real predator
items.question: explain why your brain raises fake alarms?

items.text: compare how waiting and exercise each changed your heart rate
items.question: compare how waiting and exercise changed your pulse?

items.text: weigh the cost of each kind of mistake, and test whether a calm minute brings your pulse back down
items.question: weigh the cost of each mistake, and test a calm minute?

materials: A closed box with a pinecone inside; five cones or hoops for the bushes; a start line and a safe line
Eight clue cards (page 3): three tiger clues and five wind cards, mostly leaves
A clock with a second hand; differentiated handouts and pencils
questions: Have you ever found that waiting for something was worse than the thing itself?
Why might it be safer to see a fake threat than to miss a real one?
When has your heart raced before a game, a test or a performance? What helped?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the poster
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** poster 1 and the two tactile Mystery Fear Boxes in the case. **Online:** *What Scares You?* plays the Rustling Bushes on a screen (try *Guess first* to talk each round over), and has a pulse you can tap.

steps.title: Before you touch anything
script: Seat the class. Teach the count: *“Find your pulse on your wrist or neck. Count the beats for 30 seconds, then double it: beats a minute.”* (the lab’s *Take your own pulse* asks for the wrist or neck). Everyone records a resting pulse. Then bring out the closed box. Read the poster: *“Put your hand in a box you can’t see into. Your heart races before you even touch anything. Why?”* Say that one volunteer may reach in. Everyone counts again while they wait. Then reveal it: a pinecone.

screen.question: Put your hand in a box you can’t see into. Your heart races before you even touch anything. Why?

steps.purpose: Take a resting pulse, then feel what waiting does to it.
students: Find your pulse on your wrist or neck. Count the beats for 30 seconds, then double it: beats a minute.
Now watch the box. Count again.

steps.title: Better safe than sorry
script: Read: *“When faced with uncertainty, your brain doesn’t imagine neutral scenarios—it imagines disasters. This “negativity bias” kept ancestors alive. Those who assumed rustling bushes contained tigers lived longer than optimists.”* and *“This isn’t a flaw—it’s by design. Our brains know it is better to see 100 fake threats than miss one real predator.”* Ask which costs more: a fake alarm, or a missed tiger.

screen.text: When faced with uncertainty, your brain doesn’t imagine neutral scenarios—it imagines disasters. This “negativity bias” kept ancestors alive. Those who assumed rustling bushes contained tigers lived longer than optimists.
screen.cite: Poster 1 · Your Brain Catastrophizes on Purpose

steps.purpose: Understand why the brain leans toward fake alarms.
students: Which mistake was worse for our ancestors: running from the wind, or staying put for a tiger?

steps.title: Read the clues
script: Explain the game, as the lab plays it: eight rounds, five bushes, three tigers. A bush rustles, then a clue may appear. Every tiger leaves one; the wind mostly blows leaves loose, and sometimes leaves none. You have ten seconds to call it.

screen.caption: The Rustling Bushes’ clues: every tiger leaves one; the wind mostly blows leaves loose, and sometimes leaves none

steps.purpose: Learn the game’s clue cards before playing.
students: What does it mean when there is no clue?

steps.title: Choose a data sheet
script: Students choose a data sheet. All three record four pulses and the team’s calls; Yellow and Red go on to compare and explain.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Record four pulses and color a bar for each, tally the team’s calls, and finish sentences about when the heart beat fastest and what each mistake costs.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Record four pulses, work out each change, graph them, and explain which mistake their team made more often, using poster 1.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Compare the change from waiting with the change from running, design a fairer test of waiting alone, and argue whether the game’s points match the poster’s trade-off.

steps.purpose: Each student takes the data sheet that fits, before the game.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three record your pulse and your team’s calls.

steps.title: Tiger or wind?
script: Teams line up at the start line facing five cones, the bushes. A caller stands behind one bush, rustles it, then holds up a clue card or none. Teams have ten seconds. **Tiger:** sprint to the safe line. **Wind:** stay and hold a balance. Shuffle three tiger cards and five wind cards for eight rounds.

Score each round: a team that runs from the wind makes a **fake alarm** (one point and a run for nothing); a team that stays for a tiger makes a **missed tiger** (five points). Lowest score wins. Students who would rather not run can be callers and scorers.

screen.question: Tiger or wind? You have ten seconds to decide.

steps.purpose: Play the Rustling Bushes with bodies: decide fast, and count the cost of each mistake.
students: Tiger: run to the safe line.
Wind: stay and hold your balance.
Tally every fake alarm and every missed tiger.

steps.title: Cool down and record
script: Straight after round eight, everyone takes a pulse. Then one slow, calm minute: sit, breathe slowly, eyes on the floor. Take it again. *“Find your pulse on your wrist or neck. Count the beats for 30 seconds, then double it: beats a minute.”*

screen.question: Take your pulse now. Then one slow, calm minute, and take it again.

steps.purpose: Measure what the game did to the heart, and whether a calm minute brings it down.
students: Find your pulse on your wrist or neck. Count the beats for 30 seconds, then double it: beats a minute.
Record both numbers on your sheet.

steps.title: Scared a medium amount
script: Read: *“In 2020, 110 visitors to a haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, wore heart-rate monitors. They enjoyed it most when scared a medium amount.”* Ask why scientists would measure heart rate to study a scare, and when the class’s own hearts raced today: waiting, running or both?

screen.text: In 2020, 110 visitors to a haunted house in Vejle, Denmark, wore heart-rate monitors. They enjoyed it most when scared a medium amount.
screen.cite: What Scares You? · Known or Unknown?

steps.purpose: See how real scientists used heart rate to study fear.
students: Why measure heart rate to study a haunted house?
When did your own heart race today?

steps.title: Look back
script: Then ask the objectives back as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Exit ticket: *“Which mistake did your team make more, and why?”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.
